old: Its ancestors all describe something thin, straight, and rigid — long before anyone baked with it.
In French, the word simply means "stick."
It passed through Italian bacchetta on its way from Latin baculum to French, and finally into English.
clues: This bakery staple carries a name that traces back to a Latin word for a staff or walking stick, a long way from anything you would eat.
It is a long, slender loaf with a crackly golden crust and airy inside, far longer than a dinner roll. In Italian, its ancestor simply meant a small stick.
Picture a Parisian strolling home with one tucked under an arm. Jewelers also use the same name for a slim, rectangular cut of gemstone.
